questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An essay built around a question
questions.learningObjective: explain what question an essay is organised to answer
questions.stem: An essay opens, "Nearly every handbook for this city recommends the same evening climb, and I made it three times before I could say what the climb was for." It then argues about how far a reader should trust a recommendation. What makes the piece an essay rather than a report of three walks?

options.text: The piece is built around a question it puts to itself, and the three walks are the material it uses to answer, not the thing it means to describe
The piece is written in the first person, so a reader is told the writer was present for what is reported, and that presence is what the form is defined by
options.misconception: treats a first-person voice as the defining feature of the essay, ignoring the question the piece is organised around

options.text: The piece is written to be believed, so the account of three walks counts as evidence only because the writer is prepared to stand behind every detail of it
options.misconception: makes truth the criterion, so a personal report counts as an essay because a reader can check it

options.text: The piece runs longer than a notice would, and length is the ordinary signal a reader uses to tell an argument apart from an announcement of facts
options.misconception: uses length as the marker of argument, when what marks an essay is the question it is built to answer

questions.explanation: An essay is distinguished by the question it is built to answer, and everything else in it is material for that answer. This piece names the question in its first sentence and then admits, in the same sentence, that three trips did not settle it, which tells a reader that the walking is not the point and the uncertainty is. That is why it cannot be a report: a report of three walks would end when the walks ended and would owe a reader no position. The second option takes a voice as a form, but a first-person narrator appears in reports, in letters and in apologies; what these have in common is not who speaks but what the piece is for. The third makes truth the test, and truth is a separate question that an essay may decline to claim, since an essay is measured by what it argues rather than by what it certifies. The fourth uses length as evidence, which is a property a writer can produce by any means, including padding.
questions.hint: Ask what the piece would owe a reader if it simply stopped after the third walk.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Three answers weighed as an argument
questions.learningObjective: identify an essay whose material is a set of competing answers to one question
questions.stem: A writer opens: "I do not know what the ferry is for. The timetable says it runs. The sign at the landing says it is for people going to the island. The man who sells tickets says it is for people who will want to come back." The next four paragraphs take one of these three statements at a time and measure it against the other two. What is the essay doing?

options.text: It is testing three available answers to a single question, so the writing's purpose is the testing and the three statements are the material being weighed
It is reporting what three people said on a landing, so the essay's claim is that reliable witnesses agree and a reader may safely act on it
options.misconception: takes three pieces of testimony as the conclusion, when the paragraphs measure the statements against each other

options.text: It is recording the writer's own indecision, so the argument's work is to show that a person can hold three beliefs at once without needing to choose
options.misconception: makes the writer's uncertainty the subject, which is what a paragraph about indecision would do rather than four of weighing

options.text: It is setting a timetable against a sign, so the essay is really about the difference between a printed schedule and an unsigned notice
options.misconception: narrows three weighed statements to two documents, losing the ticket seller's account of return journeys

questions.explanation: The structure tells a reader what the piece is for. Four paragraphs that each take one statement and measure it against the others are not collecting opinions; they are running a comparison, and a comparison has to end somewhere. What the essay is testing is a question the writer states in the first sentence and cannot yet answer, which is the ordinary condition of an essay that is doing work rather than reporting. Each of the three statements is a candidate answer, and the paragraphs establish why two of them fail and what the third would have to include to survive. The second option mistakes the material for the conclusion, since a set of witnesses is not a finding until the witnesses are weighed against something. The third makes the writer's state of mind the subject, which would need the essay to be about indecision rather than about a ferry's purpose. The fourth is the trap of the most concrete detail, because the timetable and the sign are only two of the three things being compared, and the third is the one the essay begins from.
questions.hint: Ask why one statement is taken at a time rather than all three together.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Memoir against autobiography
questions.learningObjective: state how a memoir differs from an autobiography in scope and selection
questions.stem: A writer's book covers the year in which her mother's village was demolished, and it is arranged by what the writer noticed at particular ages rather than by the order of events. How does the memoir's relation to a life differ from an autobiography's?

options.text: The memoir selects and arranges around a handful of remembered scenes, so it is bounded by what memory can supply rather than by the life those scenes belong to
The memoir has to be checked against a record of a whole life, since a memoir is a life written down and an autobiography is a life looked back on
options.misconception: reverses the two forms, treating the memoir as the exhaustive record and the autobiography as the selective one

options.text: The memoir is written in the present tense throughout, so it differs from an autobiography in tense rather than in the extent it takes on
options.misconception: makes tense the defining difference, when any of the forms may use any tense at any point

options.text: The memoir is written for publication while an autobiography stays private, so what separates the two is the audience rather than the design
options.misconception: grounds the difference in publication, ignoring that either form can be published or withheld

questions.explanation: The dividing line is what each form is obliged to cover. An autobiography is measured against the life it claims to record, so omissions in it are omissions from a whole, and a reader who finds a gap can complain about the gap. A memoir is measured against a stretch of experience, which means the writer is free to choose where the stretch begins and ends and to arrange what is inside it by anything other than date, including by the writer's own age at the time or by the quality of a memory. The arrangement named in the stem is the giveaway: a book ordered by the writer's age rather than by the events' order has been organised by a memory's shape. The second option reverses the pair, which is the commonest error, because the shorter book sounds like the less complete one. The third mistakes a possible stylistic choice for the definition of a form. The fourth confuses the conditions under which each form is written with what it is.
questions.hint: Ask which form is measured against a whole life and which against a chosen stretch.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two books, one memoir
questions.learningObjective: decide which of two described books is the memoir and say what decides it
questions.stem: Book A runs to nine chapters and covers its author's life from a childhood flat to a present-day job, in strict date order, with a chronology appendix. Book B runs to four chapters and stays inside one winter in which the author's father was ill, opening and closing in the same room. Which is the memoir, and what decides it?

options.text: Book B, since its span is a remembered stretch of experience it can shape, where Book A's span is the life itself and so is the autobiography's extent
Book A, since a longer book records more of a life, and length is the ordinary measure of how complete an account has managed to be
options.misconception: infers completeness from length, where a memoir is defined by selection rather than by coverage

options.text: Book B, since a memoir must be shorter than an autobiography, and the shorter of two books is therefore the one built from memory
options.misconception: gets the relation between the two forms right about size and wrong about what size is measuring

options.text: Book A, since the presence of an appendix makes the account documentary, and documentary method is what separates the two forms
options.misconception: treats an appendix as decisive, when the deciding question is the extent the book takes on

questions.explanation: The two descriptions are built so that one signal each is misleading, and the deciding signal is the span. Book A's span is a life, from a first home to a present job, in date order, and a life covered from beginning to present in date order is what an autobiography is for. Book B's span is one winter, bounded at both ends by events rather than by birth and employment, and it opens and closes in a single room, which is a shape memory can hold and a whole life cannot. The second option reads length as completeness, and completeness is exactly the claim a memoir does not make about itself. The third sounds right because the books do differ in size, but the size is a consequence of the span rather than the definition of the form, and an autobiography can be brief and a memoir can be long. The fourth makes an appendix decisive; an appendix is a convenience for checking dates, and a memoir may include one while remaining a memory.
questions.hint: Ask which book's boundaries are events and which book's boundaries are a life.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A travelogue's method of looking
questions.learningObjective: describe the observational method a travelogue passage is using
questions.stem: A traveller's book spends a page on a market. It does not give the market's size or its prices. It records what could be heard from three stalls, which stall the traveller approached first, and what she was looking for when she chose it. What method is the passage using?

options.text: It is selecting observations that answer a question set before arrival, so the noticing is chosen against a question rather than gathered for its own sake
It is describing the market comprehensively, so the three stalls stand in for the whole and a reader is handed a usable account of the place
options.misconception: takes a question-led selection for coverage, so a partial record is read as a summary of the whole place

options.text: It is recording events in the order they occurred, so the approach to the stalls reconstructs the morning as it actually unfolded
options.misconception: reads a chosen sequence as chronology, when the order records where the traveller looked rather than when things happened

options.text: It is comparing this market with others in other towns, so the detail about the first stall is chosen because a second market will contrast with it
options.misconception: supposes a comparison the passage never names, sets up or completes

questions.explanation: The three details chosen tell a reader what the traveller was doing, and what she was doing was checking something. Stalls are heard from rather than counted, an order of approach is recorded, and a purpose is named, and all three of those belong to an observer who arrived with a question rather than one who is filling a page. That is the working method of travel writing at its best: a question produces a selection, and the selection can disappoint the traveller, which is what makes the writing report something. The second option reads a narrow record as a wide one, and a market described by three stalls is not thereby a market described. The third confuses the order in which a writer looks with the order in which things happen, and the two are independent. The fourth supplies a comparison the passage does not make; a second market never appears, and a detail is not evidence of a contrast until the contrast is on the page.
questions.hint: Ask why a market was described by what was heard from three stalls rather than by what it contained.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An opening question used as a test
questions.learningObjective: explain how a travelogue chapter turns received advice into evidence
questions.stem: A travelogue's fourth chapter opens, "Everyone tells you the market is early, so I went at six to see whether it was, and the answer is that it is early and that this has nothing to do with why." The chapter then describes an hour in which nothing was sold. What is the chapter doing with the opening question?

options.text: It is converting received advice into a test, so the hour of waiting becomes evidence about the advice rather than a description of a market
It is establishing the traveller's expertise at the outset, so the reader is prepared to take the later description as a professional judgement
options.misconception: reads self-description as expertise, which the word but in the same sentence already puts in doubt

options.text: It is introducing the market as a character, so the hour without sales gives the place a personality the chapter then goes on to develop
options.misconception: personifies the market, when what the chapter examines is an answer rather than a character

options.text: It is setting up a contrast between morning and evening, so the later pages compare two trading hours by what each of them produces
options.misconception: supposes a two-hour comparison, whereas the chapter narrows to one hour and one piece of advice

questions.explanation: The opening contains the method in full, and the method is a trial. The traveller takes a thing everybody says, states what everybody says it for, goes to find out, and then answers in a form that separates the two parts of the claim: the market is early, yes, and that is not the reason anything should be told. A chapter that then spends an hour watching nothing sell is gathering the evidence for that split, and an hour in which nothing happens is evidence precisely because nobody's advice predicted it. The second option is the trap the sentence builds for a careless reader, since the phrase about going to see is what sounds like expertise, and the concession that follows is what shows the going did not produce it. The third turns a claim about cause into a character, and a personality cannot be examined by an hour of failed trading. The fourth invents a second hour; nothing in the opening promises an evening, and the chapter's whole point is that a morning of nothing settles the question.
questions.hint: Ask what the word but does to the answer the traveller arrives at.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Sustained attention to a small site
questions.learningObjective: describe the kind of attention a nature essay gives a single site
questions.stem: A nature essay describes one square metre of a riverbank across a year, and it records not the landscape but the dates on which a particular stone was submerged and uncovered. What kind of attention is this?

options.text: It is sustained attention to a small site at repeated intervals, so what accumulates is the pattern the place makes rather than the scene it presents
It is close description of a single moment, since fixing one place and one detail is what makes any description exact enough to be of use
options.misconception: collapses a year of visits into one moment, which removes the interval that is the essay's actual subject

options.text: It is scientific monitoring, since the dates of submersion are measurements, and a measurement is the strongest form evidence can take
options.misconception: takes measurement as decisive, ignoring that the subject is what the intervals mean rather than what they record

options.text: It is landscape appreciation, since the pleasure of a riverbank is best served by returning to it and noticing more each time a season turns
options.misconception: reduces the piece to pleasure, whereas what accumulates across the year is knowledge rather than delight

questions.explanation: Three conditions are present together and it takes all three to name the method: the site is small, the site is the same, and the visits are spread over a year. Fixing one place gives the essay its object, returning gives it a series, and the series is what produces a pattern rather than an impression. A stone that is covered and uncovered on dated occasions is the sort of thing that can only be known by comparison across time, and the essay's subject is therefore the comparison. The second option reduces the series to a moment, which loses precisely the thing that took a year to acquire; a single precise description of a stone is a different piece of writing. The third is the trap that looks hardest-working, but a date is a measurement only in the sense that a temperature is, and the essay is not doing physics with it. The fourth makes the motive pleasure, and a reader who reads the piece for delight will find very little of it here.
questions.hint: Ask what the essay would have if it visited the site only once.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A description tested against a second visit
questions.learningObjective: analyse how a nature essay uses a later season to check an earlier description
questions.stem: A nature essay's fourth paragraph reads: "In August the bank is one colour and the water is another and the two do not argue. In February the water is the colour of the bank's shadow, and the paragraph I would have to write to describe February would be the same paragraph with a river in it." What is that sentence doing?

options.text: It is setting the second season against the first description, so February is used to find out whether the August account held rather than to take its place
It is describing two seasons in order, so the reader is given a sequence of appearances and the sequence itself is what the essay is about
options.misconception: treats the sequence as the subject, when the second season is put to work on the first description

options.text: It is making a claim about colour, so February confirms August and the essay's argument turns out to be a claim about rivers
options.misconception: reduces the passage to a general claim about appearance and ignores the test being applied to the writer's own words

options.text: It is conceding that description fails, so the essay admits its method cannot carry a second season and leaves the question of method open
options.misconception: reads self-doubt as a failure of method, when the sentence is the method succeeding

questions.explanation: The second season is an experiment, and the experiment is run on the writer's own first description. August gives a relation between bank and water, a relation the paragraph says the two hold without struggle, and February is then described as a relation that would make the same sentence work if the parts were swapped. What is being asked is whether the August account was a description of a place or only a description of a month, and the answer is produced by the second visit rather than asserted. The second option reads a pair of descriptions as a sequence and stops, which loses the test entirely; nothing in the paragraph needs the first to come second except the comparison. The third mistakes the result for the subject: the passage does reach a claim about how two seasons sit together, but it reaches that claim by checking a description, and a claim about colour alone would need no second visit. The fourth is the trap of a modest-sounding sentence. The hypothetical paragraph is not an admission that the method failed; it is the method, because a description that survives being applied to a different month is the one a reader can use.
questions.hint: Ask what work the second season is put to besides being described.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A lyric essay that argues about its own lack of grounds
questions.learningObjective: describe the argument a lyric essay makes through its images
questions.stem: A lyric essay opens with three images that explain nothing and states no position until its ninth paragraph, where the images are called "what I have instead of a reason". What is the essay arguing?

options.text: That its images and the position they reach are a substitute for a reason, so the claim being made is about what the essay has got in place of grounds
That a position needed building first, so the ninth paragraph begins reasoning and the images are illustrations of the reasoning that follows it
options.misconception: reads the essay as a delayed argument, when the ninth paragraph states that the usual ground is missing

options.text: That argument is not available to it, so the ninth paragraph announces a subject and the images turn out to be decoration around it
options.misconception: takes the absence of an early position as the absence of an argument, ignoring the claim made at the ninth paragraph

options.text: That private experience generalises, so the ninth paragraph draws a rule from the particular case that the three images supply
options.misconception: supposes a general rule is being produced, which the ninth paragraph explicitly denies

questions.explanation: The ninth paragraph is the essay's thesis, and its content decides what kind of essay this is. What the images are said to be is a substitute for a reason, which means the essay is not short of a position but short of grounds, and it is about that shortage. A lyric essay reaches a position by accumulating images until the accumulation can bear weight, and the moment it becomes clear what the images are for, the piece has made a claim that can be disagreed with, which is the test a position has to pass. The second option is the reading the ninth paragraph is written to defeat, because it treats the images as support for reasoning that the essay has said it does not have. The third hears a refusal of argument where there is a refusal of one kind of argument, and the ninth paragraph is not a subject announcement, since a subject could have been stated in the first. The fourth supplies a generalisation the text disclaims in the same clause that names its images.
questions.hint: Ask what the ninth paragraph claims the three images are for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: One opening sentence, two kinds of essay
questions.learningObjective: compare two continuations of the same sentence and identify what each essay argues
questions.stem: Two essays open with the same sentence: "The clock in my grandmother's kitchen was five minutes fast for thirty years." A goes on to argue about how accuracy ought to be judged. B goes on to list every repair the owner made, in order, over the thirty years. Which comparison best accounts for the difference between them?

options.text: A turns the detail into a claim about judgement, while B keeps the detail as a record, so the two essays are built to answer different questions
A and B differ only in length, since a single sentence can be developed at any length without changing what the essay is doing with it
options.misconception: assumes the opening sentence fixes the essay's kind, ignoring what the second paragraph is for

options.text: A is better founded because it reaches a general claim, while B's list of repairs is evidence that cannot support a general claim at all
options.misconception: dismisses B's list as unusable evidence, where a list of repairs can show a habit rather than a set of anecdotes

options.text: A and B are making the same claim about drift, and the difference is only that A states it early and B makes a reader wait for the repairs
options.misconception: sees one claim expressed twice, when A generalises about judgement and B reports what happened

questions.explanation: The same sentence can carry two essays only if the second paragraph tells a reader which question the sentence is being used to ask. A takes the five minutes as a case against measuring a clock against a standard, so its subject is a judgment and its evidence is one household. B takes the thirty years as a stretch to be covered, so its subject is the sequence of interventions and its order is the order in which they were made. The difference is therefore not one of degree or length but of what the material is for, which is the question a first sentence always leaves open. The second option treats a shared opening as a shared essay, and length would not settle it in any case. The third assumes that only general claims can be founded, and a list of repairs is strong evidence of a habit that a reader can check against the clock's behaviour. The fourth is the most natural error, because both essays do concern a clock, but a claim about how accuracy should be judged is not a claim about when a part was replaced.
questions.hint: Ask what the second paragraph is for in each of the two essays.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What makes an account a process
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a process account from a narrative of events
questions.stem: A process essay describes how a writer salvaged a drowned notebook. It gives a decision to stop, a decision to dry the pages, and a decision to leave the ink alone, and it says the first decision was forced by the clock and the second by the paper's condition. What makes the sequence a process rather than a story?

options.text: Each step is settled by a condition the writer can state and could have judged otherwise, so the order carries reasoning rather than mere succession
The steps occur one after another in time, so the order of the events is what tells a reader an account is a process and not something else
options.misconception: grounds process in time alone, which would make any list of events a process

options.text: The steps belong to the writer and were carried out alone, so personal ownership of the method is what makes the account a process
options.misconception: uses the writer's ownership as the test, where what makes a process is a stateable condition at each step

options.text: Another reader could repeat the steps on a different notebook, so an account counts as a process exactly when it can be transferred
options.misconception: assumes transferability is the point, though a process essay can describe a method that works only once

questions.explanation: The essay's own sentence supplies the test, and the test is about conditions rather than about time. Each decision is paired with something the writer could have named: a clock, a paper's condition, an ink that had not yet dried. Where a decision has a condition behind it, a reader can ask whether the condition justified it, and that question is the whole content of a process essay. A story gives an order without giving grounds, and the reader of a story asks what happened next rather than whether the next thing was available. The second option is the tempting reduction, because sequence is visibly present in both a story and a process, and taking it as the test makes the two indistinguishable. The third confuses who acts with what kind of account results; the same steps can be reported by an observer. The fourth makes transferability the definition, which would exclude the many process essays that describe something done once and never again, and transferability is a claim about usefulness rather than about form.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could ask about each step that they could not ask about an event in a story.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Process steps restored to their order
questions.learningObjective: restore a process essay's steps so each condition precedes the step it governs
questions.stem: Four steps from an invented process essay have been printed in the wrong order. Restore them so that each step's condition has already been established by the step before it.

options.text: and then I set the page on a stone in the shade
and I found the water still in the gutter, which is where the book had gone
and the wind came round the corner of the yard and lifted the corner
and I did not open it, which is the decision I still think was right

questions.explanation: Each step states a condition, and each condition is created by the step before it, which makes the order recoverable rather than a matter of opinion. The book is found first, because until it is in the gutter there is nothing to dry and nothing has been ruined. The wind comes next, and it comes next because the book is in the open and has been open long enough for a gust to reach the corner of it; that gust is what lifts the corner and what makes drying the obvious next concern. Drying then comes third, and it is a step that needs the corner to have been lifted, since a soaked page under a wet corner is not a page that can be dried. The decision not to open comes last, and it is last because it is the decision the earlier steps make necessary: once the paper has dried in the shade and the wind has already taken the corner, opening it would be the first irreversible act. The order printed in the stem puts the fourth step first, which is why the conditions seemed to arrive after the decisions they were supposed to govern.
questions.hint: Find the step that has to happen before any of the others can be described at all.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Extending a definition by a case it cannot hold
questions.learningObjective: identify the mechanism a definition essay uses to extend a definition
questions.stem: A definition essay opens, "A hedge is a boundary," and then spends its remaining four pages on the cases where that definition is nearly useless. What extension mechanism is the essay using?

options.text: It is extending the standard definition by producing cases the definition cannot cover, so the extension is an addition the definition could not make for itself
It is extending the definition by restating it in several sentences, so the added sense is produced by repetition until the term feels secure in the mouth
options.misconception: makes repetition the mechanism, where the four pages are spent on cases the definition cannot hold

options.text: It is extending the definition by substituting the essayist's own, so the added sense comes from replacement and the accepted meaning is discarded
options.misconception: describes substitution as extension, when the accepted sense is kept and enlarged

options.text: It is extending the definition by collecting dictionaries, so the added sense is the number of authorities behind the term and not any case it misses
options.misconception: counts authorities instead of testing coverage, which is the essay's actual method

questions.explanation: Four pages on cases is a method, and the method has a name in the writing of definitions: a definition is extended by finding something it fails to cover and saying what the failure shows. A boundary that cannot deal with the hedges the essay describes has been shown to be incomplete, and the reader is then invited to say what the added sense is, which is a claim the essay can argue about. The second option is the opposite of what is happening, since four pages of application cannot be produced by restating the same sentence. The third makes extension a matter of replacement, but a definition essay that simply substituted a new sense would have no use for the old one, and the fact that the essay begins with the accepted sense shows it intends to keep it. The fourth mistakes the gathering of authorities for the testing of coverage, which is the trap of an essay that has a shelf of references behind it and no case that any of them explains.
questions.hint: Ask what a definition essay has to produce if it is going to be more than a repetition.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A definition extended and where it stops
questions.learningObjective: explain how a definition essay uses two cases to set a limit on its own extension
questions.stem: A definition essay begins, "A debt, in law, is money owed." Its second page turns to a credit card, which the essay says is a debt in every ordinary use but is not money owed to the person who holds the card. Its third page turns to a wager between two neighbours about rain, which is money owed on a condition and which nobody calls a debt. Explain what the essay is doing to the definition, and why the wager matters more than the credit card.

answer.exemplar: The essay is not replacing the definition, it is asking how far the definition reaches, and it uses two cases that fail in the same formal way in order to find where the difference lies. Both the card and the wager are money owed by someone to someone else who is not the person holding the obligation, and if the essay had stopped at the structural resemblance, both would count as debts and the definition would be widened into uselessness. What separates them is not the structure but the agreement of speakers: people in fact call the card a debt and do not call the wager a debt, and the essay is arguing that this ordinary consent is the test a case has to pass before a definition is obliged to stretch. The card therefore does the easy work, because it supplies a case where the definition is too narrow and usage insists on the wider sense, and the wager does the harder work, because it supplies a case of identical form that usage refuses, which is what tells a reader where to stop. An explanation worth the name has to say both: that the mechanism is a counter-instance tested against ordinary consent, and that the second case is the more instructive because it costs the essay its own rule if the rule is stated only as resemblance. The example above says what the two cases share, what the test is, and why the weaker case does more work than the stronger one, because an account that stopped at the credit card would describe an extension without showing where an extension may end.

questions.explanation: An explanation of a definitional essay has to name the mechanism and then name the limit, because an extension with no limit is not a finding but a preference. The mechanism here is a counter-instance admitted on the strength of ordinary consent rather than on formal resemblance, and a reader who cannot state that test cannot tell whether the card or the wager belongs. The limit is the harder half, because the wager is the case the essay's own logic would have to exclude, and excluding it requires saying that usage can refuse a case that structurally fits. It has committed to finding a single difference, so a comparison that turns up two differences at once has failed to keep to the basis it declared
options.misconception: makes a basis a limit on findings, when it is a lens the essay applies to everything it turns up

options.text: It has committed to a feature both markets share, since a basis of comparison must be a property of each rather than a property of one alone
options.misconception: requires a shared feature, which would rule out comparing by a property only one of the pair has

options.text: It has committed to the smaller market, on the convention that an essay beginning with the less frequent case is by definition writing about an exception
options.misconception: reads a convention about order into the choice, where the interval is a subject rather than a courtesy

B's, because a difference in the order of information is easier for a reader to check than any judgement about a narrator's reliability
options.misconception: prefers the checkable fact over the substantive judgement, which reverses what a basis of comparison is for

options.text: A's, because comparisons by technique are always more substantial than comparisons by structure, and reliability is a technique

The third asserts a hierarchy of bases that the pair exists to complicate, and it also misdescribes reliability, which is an effect produced by a narrator's relation to what happened rather than a technique. A third decade, since a claim of cause cannot rest on a single pattern and repetition of the pattern is the only thing that would make it safe
options.misconception: thinks the cure is more instances of the correlation, which would leave the causal claim unsupported however many there were

options.text: A named witness, since readers distrust figures and will accept a measurement only when someone is found who remembers the hours accurately
options.misconception: substitutes authority to remember for a warrant, and a witness does not connect later hours to fewer loans

options.text: A definition of borrowing, since the meaning of the statistic is unsettled and no causal claim can be assessed until the term is fixed
options.misconception: moves to terminology, which cannot supply the missing link between two measured facts

The fourth turns to terminology, which is a real concern for any statistic and still cannot perform the work of connecting cause to effect.

A third closure, since two events in sequence are too short to be a pattern and a causal claim has to have a pattern under it
options.misconception: asks for a repetition of the symptom rather than of the link that would explain it

options.text: Evidence that people walked to the village before 2019, since the claim assumes a habit that the essay has not yet shown anyone had
options.misconception: asks for the wrong half, because even a documented habit would not connect the shop's closure to it

options.text: Corrected dates, since a causal claim is only as good as the chronology it rests on and a wrong year would undo the whole of it
options.misconception: treats accuracy as sufficient, and an accurate sequence still says nothing about cause

What is missing is a link, and a link is a thing about the world rather than about the calendar: that people who needed one shop bought elsewhere, that the bakery's customers had already stopped coming, that a bus route ended in the same month. The third establishes a habit without relating it to the shop, so even if the walk is documented the causal claim would be untouched. questions.stem: An essay argues that a town should keep its weekly market in the car park instead of moving it to the rebuilt square. The paragraph before the conclusion sets out the square's advantages at length. What is that paragraph for?

options.text: It is the strongest available objection, stated as well as it could be stated, so the essay can answer the best case rather than the easiest one
It is a concession the essay has to make, so the reader sees the writer is fair before the final decision is announced at the end
options.misconception: reduces a counterargument to a gesture of fairness, which is what a one-sided account of the square would be

options.text: It is a delaying tactic, so the reader is given time to settle down before the essay arrives at the position it began from
options.misconception: treats the length of the paragraph as hesitation, when the paragraph is doing argumentative work

options.text: It is a summary of the square's history, so the reader knows what the square was before the argument about where the market should go
options.misconception: misreads the content as background, though the paragraph argues for the square's advantages

questions.explanation: A position essay is judged by what it does with the case against it, and the paragraph in question is that case stated in its strongest form. A market in a car park is convenient, covered, visible from the road and already there; a square in the rebuilt town is permanent, has room to sit and would be used by people who do not currently come at all. These are good reasons, and an essay that mentions them weakly has conceded nothing, because a reader who can see the weakness will repair it in their own favour. The paragraph's job is to remove that repair: it gives the objection at full strength so that the answer has to meet it. The second option is the reading this paragraph is designed to punish, since fairness is not a matter of appearing fair but of taking the opponent's best case seriously enough to answer it. The third mistakes rhetorical pressure for indecision, and a paragraph can be long because the objection is strong. The fourth is the content misread as background; an account of the square's advantages is not a history, and the essay is arguing about a market.

questions.learningObjective: analyse how a conclusion absorbs a counterargument without dropping the position

options.text: It has conceded what the objection gets right and kept the position, so the position survives the objection instead of being withdrawn by it
It has abandoned the position, since the car park's habit is the argument the essay was making and the square was only ever a weaker case
options.misconception: reads a concession as a defeat, although the writer keeps the square and qualifies the claim

options.text: It has restated the position and added a second reason, so the objection has been turned into further support for the same choice
options.misconception: misses the objection, which the word but introduces and does not fold into support

options.text: It has set the objection aside, since the clause about the habit describes the car park rather than giving a reason to prefer it
options.misconception: treats a stated reason as a description, which removes the sentence's argumentative work

questions.explanation: The sentence is built as a concession followed by a qualification, and both halves are needed to see what has happened. The third describes a different sentence, one that folded the objection into a second reason for the same choice, which is not what but is doing here. The fourth is the trap of the word and: a habit offered as a reason is still a reason, and treating it as a description is what lets a reader think the objection was never engaged.

questions.stem: A narrative non-fiction book recreates a single conversation the writer had with a stranger as though it were heard, and the writer adds, "I have set down what I am certain of and left out the rest." What truth constraint is that technique operating under?

options.text: A scene may be reconstructed only as far as the writer could afterwards stand behind its details, so invention reaches the arrangement and not the content
The scene must be approved by everyone who was present, so a reconstruction is admissible only when the other participants confirm the account afterwards
options.misconception: requires the approval of participants, which is a permission the technique itself does not confer

options.text: A detail may be supplied where a silence falls, since a reader cannot detect one and the truth of a scene lies in the effect it has on a reader
options.misconception: licenses invention because it cannot be detected, which is the opposite of the limit a reconstruction works under

options.text: The writer's memory settles every question, so where a note and a recollection conflict the note is set aside in favour of what the writer remembers
options.misconception: makes memory the final authority, ignoring that the writer's stated rule subordinates recollection to certainty

questions.explanation: The sentence written into the book is a statement of the rule, and the rule is a limit on content. What may not be arranged in is a detail the writer cannot stand behind, which is why the note about what has been left out is not a boast of modest scruple but the definition of the form. The third states the constraint backwards, since the point of a limit on invention is that the writer cannot rely on the reader's inability to detect it. options.text: It narrows the claim from transcription to reconstruction, so the sentence is being offered as a shape memory supplies rather than as a record of the words used
It withdraws the scene, since a dialogue that cannot be trusted word for word is no use as evidence of how the conversation went
options.misconception: treats one qualified detail as cancelling the whole scene, when a truth constraint bounds a claim rather than voiding it

options.text: It strengthens the chapter, since a writer who names one uncertainty has thereby assured the reader that the rest of the account is sound
options.misconception: reads an admission of uncertainty as a certificate of reliability, which reverses what candour about one detail proves

options.text: It transfers the judgement to the reader, who must now decide how much of the chapter to accept without being told how much is at issue
options.misconception: makes the reader the judge of a stated limit, when the limit is stated precisely enough to be used

Before it, a reader could take the line as a record: these words, in this sequence, were said. After it, the claim is narrower and still usable, because the words are the friend's and the order is the writer's reconstruction of how a conversation that happened would be remembered. Everything the scene is doing survives, and what has been removed is one expectation a reader was invited to hold and should not have held. The third is the natural inversion and it is how candour gets mistaken for accuracy; naming one doubt says nothing at all about the rest. The fourth describes a vaguer text; the writer has said which part is uncertain, and a reader who knows can weigh that part and the rest differently.

questions.stem: A journalist builds a profile from four recorded interviews with a council officer, and the first paragraph explains that the officer asked to see the passages attributed to her before publication. What licence is the interview material being used under?

options.text: An agreement about how the material may be used, made before publication, so what the writer may print is bounded by what was agreed rather than by what was said
A professional courtesy, so the request is a matter of etiquette and the writer may decline it without any loss of standing in the trade
options.misconception: treats an agreement about use as a matter of etiquette, when what was asked for is a limit on what may be printed

options.text: A legal permission, so the presence of a recording removes every question of consent and leaves only the question of accuracy to be checked

options.text: An exclusive arrangement, so the interview belongs to the writer until some other paper pays the same subject for the same account
options.misconception: supposes an exclusivity that nothing in the account says was offered or accepted

An officer who asks to see the passages about her is not being polite; she is asking to know the terms on which her words will be used, and a writer who agrees has obtained a licence whose content is exactly those terms. Everything afterwards in the article is measured against it, and a passage that could not have been agreed to, or that was agreed to and then changed, is a passage the writer has exceeded. The second option reduces a limit to a manner, and it leaves the officer with nothing she can enforce. The third is the commonest confusion in the trade, because a recording feels like consent; it is the opposite, since it is a record of a person saying things before anyone has said what will be done with them. The fourth invents a bargain about ownership, and no exclusivity is mentioned in either direction.

options.text: One habit of the writer and one preference of the reader, since the review divides its praise between the author and the person reviewing
options.misconception: splits the judgment into author and reader, although the sentence judges the book on both counts

questions.explanation: The sentence marks each criterion with a phrase that tells a reader how to price it. Careful with money is credited as rare, and rarity is a fact about other books rather than about this one, so the credit is real but modest; careless with time is a different kind of remark entirely, because the phrase which matters more here says the quality is required by the book's own subject. A novel about an estate's accounts cannot survive mishandled time, whereas a novel about an estate's accounts can be merely unremarkable about money. That is what a weighted criterion is, and it is the difference between saying a book is good in general and saying what this book had to do well. The second option would have it that a review may not have priorities, which would leave a reader unable to predict anything about a judgment. The third mistakes two applications of one word for one test, when care and carelessness are opposites and the sentence needs them to be opposites. The fourth assigns the two remarks to different people, and both are about the book.
questions.hint: Ask what the book needed to get right, as opposed to what would merely have been impressive.

questions.topic: What kind of claim a critical essay makes
questions.learningObjective: identify the kind of claim a critical essay makes about a text
questions.stem: A critical essay says of an invented novel, "The last chapter repeats the opening scene with two people missing from it, and the repetitions are so exact that no one could be added without being noticed." What kind of claim is being made?

options.text: A claim about a pattern in the text and about what the pattern can be made to do, so a reader could test it against the two chapters it describes
A claim about what the novel means, so the last chapter is being read as the statement of a meaning the earlier chapters were leading towards
options.misconception: reads a claim about a pattern as a claim about what the whole book means

options.text: A claim about the novel's quality, so the exactness of the repetition is offered as proof that the book is more carefully made than its rivals
options.misconception: turns a textual observation into a verdict on the book's worth

options.text: A claim about the novel's effect on readers, so the two absent people are described in order to account for how the book makes a reader finish it
options.misconception: shifts to the reader's experience, though the evidence offered is about the text's own arrangement

questions.explanation: The claim is bounded by what a reader could do with it, and the sentence invites a specific action: take the two chapters and see whether the absences really are unnoticeable, which is a thing about the text that can be checked in an afternoon. questions.hint: Ask what a reader would have to do to check the sentence.

questions.topic: An inconsistency claim against a writing claim

questions.stem: Essay A argues, "The second narrator's account of the fire supplies a detail no witness at the scene had any way of seeing, and the book has made no effort to hide the impossibility." options.text: A is about what the text could have known and B is about how the prose performs, so the second cannot settle the first and the first does not touch the second
A and B are making the same claim about one narrator, since a passage that cannot be true is a passage that has not been well written
options.misconception: conflates the two questions, which is what a single narrator's slip is regularly taken to show

options.text: A measures accuracy while B measures effect, so the two are simply two scales for a single judgement about the quality of the book
options.misconception: reduces both to judgements of quality, when one of them concerns a text's relation to a possible world

options.text: B is the stronger claim, since quality is a property a reader can feel and what a narrator could have seen is a matter of conjecture about a fire
options.misconception: supposes a reader can settle what a narrator could have seen, which is exactly what is in dispute

questions.explanation: Two questions are being asked of the same passage and they answer to different evidence. The second option treats an impossibility as a defect of prose, which is the assumption A is contesting by insisting the book has not hidden it. The third reduces a pair of questions to one scale, and the fourth gets the evidential relation backwards by assuming a reader's impression of quality can adjudicate what a witness could perceive.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence each claim would need that the other does not have.

questions.topic: The limit of the personal in a personal essay
questions.learningObjective: state what bounds the personal in a personal essay
questions.stem: A personal essay about the author's mother's death names her, names the hospital, and quotes a conversation held two days before she died. What governs how far the personal may go?

options.text: What the people it names would recognise, so the question at each stage is whether a detail enlarges the essay's claim at a cost its subject did not choose to bear
The law of defamation, so an essay may report anything true about a living person and may report anything at all about a person who is dead
options.misconception: reduces a moral question to a legal one, and a legal test does not settle what a dying woman in a hospital would have wished for

options.text: The author's own permission, since an adult may tell what happened within their own family and needs nobody's agreement to do so
options.misconception: assumes the author's ownership of the material settles it, though the material is not only about the author

options.text: The convention that a family belongs to an essayist, so naming a parent is ordinary and the question of recognition never arises
options.misconception: invents a convention that removes the question the essay exists to raise

questions.explanation: A personal essay is not a diary, and the difference is that its material is held in common with somebody else. Every named hospital and every quoted sentence is recognisable to at least one person who did not choose to be in print, and the essay has to get something from that which is worth what it asks of them. The recognisability test is the one a writer can actually apply, because it does not require knowing what a person would have wanted and only requires noticing whether they could tell it is about them. The third is the belief that trips writers most often, and it is understandable, because the writer was there; but the conversation quoted was not the writer's alone, and the author's authority over the memory does not extend over the other's part in it. The fourth is a convention the essay form has no such need of, and adopting it is a way of not asking.
questions.hint: Ask who else would recognise the detail being printed.

questions.topic: Letting an unfair sentence stand
questions.learningObjective: analyse the limit a personal essay negotiates when it reports an unfair judgement
questions.stem: A personal essay about an argument with a brother reads, "He said, and I am quoting him, that I had never once asked him for anything. That is not true, and it is not false either, and I have decided to let it stand." Which limit is the essay negotiating?

options.text: The limit of what one person may claim about another, since the essay prints a sentence it knows to be unfair and declines to correct it in the text
The limit of what a reader can be expected to follow, since the remark about asking is hard to place and the essay chooses not to explain it further
options.misconception: makes the difficulty a matter of the reader's patience, when it is a difficulty about what is true

options.text: The limit of what may be said about family in print, since the brother is named in an essay about him and the sentence could not stand without his agreement
options.misconception: assumes the brother agreed to the printing, which the presence of the sentence does not establish

options.text: The limit of the essay's own length, since the author records the decision and moves on, and a longer account would be about him rather than about her
options.misconception: treats a restraint about truth as a question of length

questions.explanation: The sentence is deliberately unresolved, and the resolution would undo the essay. That her brother never once asked is not true, because there are occasions the essay has not reported, and it is not false either, because there are occasions on which she did not ask and notices what it cost him. The essay's position is that both halves stand, which means the sentence is unfair and true, and a text that printed the correction would be making an argument she is refusing to make about a person who is not present to answer it. What is being negotiated is therefore the claim she is entitled to make about him, not the reader's ability to follow her or the length of the piece. The third assumes a consent that the excerpt neither states nor implies, and if the brother had agreed to be named the essay would have no difficulty here. The fourth mistakes a decision about truth for a decision about proportion.
questions.hint: Ask what a correction in the text would do to the argument.

questions.topic: What a reflective opening supplies
questions.learningObjective: identify the work a reflective opening paragraph does
questions.stem: An essay's second paragraph reads, "I was thirty-one, and the letter had been in my coat for a month, and I had learned to sleep through the post." What is this paragraph supplying that the essay needs?

options.text: The conditions under which the argument is made, so a later claim is understood as something a person in that situation would claim and not as a claim from nowhere
The reader's interest, since a letter unopened and a habit of sleeping are established as the kind of detail the essay will make use of later on
options.misconception: makes the paragraph a matter of holding attention, when its work is to fix a set of conditions

options.text: The evidence the essay will argue from, since a month of not opening the letter is the material a later paragraph draws its conclusion out of
options.misconception: assumes the details are the evidence, though the evidence the argument rests on arrives later

options.text: The register the essay will keep, so a reader can learn in the second paragraph what kind of writing to expect and stop if it is not the kind wanted
options.misconception: treats the paragraph as a signal about style, when what it supplies is a situation

questions.explanation: Three facts of one kind are given, and the kind is what tells a reader the paragraph's function: an age, a duration, an acquired habit. Each fixes a circumstance, and circumstance is what an argument needs before it is made, because a claim tells a reader almost nothing until they know who is claiming it and from where. The third is the tempting error, since an unused detail does look decorative, but the paragraph establishes the ground the argument will claim ground on, and the evidence proper comes later. The fourth makes the paragraph about style, and nothing in it tells a reader about the writing.
questions.hint: Ask what a claim in the essay would need to be true about the writer to be intelligible.

questions.topic: An opening that supplies no context
questions.learningObjective: identify the paragraph left to do the work an opening has not done
questions.stem: An essay's first paragraph consists of one sentence: "Everything changed that summer." The second paragraph begins, "The policy was therefore unjust." Which paragraph is left to do the work the opening has not done?

options.text: The second, since the opening gave a season and no situation, and a claim about a policy cannot be weighed until a reader knows what the policy was and who it caught
The first, since an announcement that everything has changed is already a substantial context and the second sentence can simply refer back to it
options.misconception: assumes a general announcement supplies a situation, which is exactly what it does not do

options.text: Neither, since the two between them are sufficient: one supplies the period and the other supplies the judgment made about it
options.misconception: counts the two paragraphs instead of asking whether a reader can assess the claim

options.text: The second, since the opening gave the weather, and weather is the context a claim about a policy is most often about
options.misconception: supplies a context the text never mentions

questions.explanation: A reader reaching therefore has nothing to attach it to, and the therefore is the diagnosis. Everything changed that summer gives a season, an intensifier and a pronoun whose referent has not been named, and none of those is a situation a claim can be weighed against. The second paragraph is therefore left holding the whole argumentative labour: what the policy was, whom it fell on, and what would have to be true for the policy to be unjust rather than merely disliked. It may well perform that labour later in the paragraph, and the item's subject is the fact that it has to. The second option is the reading a reader who wants to be fair to the writer will offer, and it can be disproved by asking what changed; the sentence names no change, so nothing has been supplied that a later sentence can refer back to. The third counts paragraphs and assumes adequacy, and adequacy is a matter of what a reader can do with them. The fourth imports a context, since the text has said nothing about weather.
questions.hint: Ask what the word therefore is attached to.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An instance that carries an abstraction
questions.learningObjective: explain what a long concrete instance does for the claim that follows it
questions.stem: An essay on reading habits spends three pages on one man who carries a book he has no intention of reading, and only then states its claim, that most non-reading is settled before reading begins. What are the three pages for?

options.text: To give the claim a case, so the reader meets the mechanism as a thing happening to somebody before the mechanism is named as a general truth
To postpone the claim, so the reader is given material enough to be convinced before anything is asserted and cannot afterwards doubt the writer
options.misconception: reads the material before the claim as rhetorical strategy, when the case is doing evidentiary work

options.text: To persuade by feeling, so the reader is brought round to a position the essay holds rather than shown the position it has earned
options.misconception: reduces an instance to an appeal, though a case is a way of establishing a general claim rather than of taking its place

options.text: To restrict the claim, so the three pages limit what the later general statement can honestly be taken to cover in the world
options.misconception: treats the case as a limit on the claim, when a case is what makes a general claim intelligible

questions.explanation: A claim this large, that most non-reading is decided before reading begins, would be cheap if it were merely asserted, and the three pages are what stand between it and cheapness. A man carrying a book he does not intend to read exhibits the mechanism in a form a reader can picture: the decision has already been made, at the shelf, and everything later is theatre. Having seen the case work, the reader can hear the generalisation as a pattern rather than as an assertion, and the essay's claim is now a claim somebody has demonstrated rather than declared. The second option mistakes a structure for a stratagem; a delay is not what makes the later sentence credible, the demonstration is, and an essay that delayed without demonstrating would be empty. The third is the standard objection to case-based argument and it inverts the relation, because an instance does not replace reasoning with feeling, it supplies the specific content a generalisation otherwise lacks. The fourth reverses the case again: an instance is what licenses the claim, not what limits it.
questions.hint: Ask what the claim would be worth if the three pages were replaced by an assertion of confidence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two instances of one claim compared
questions.learningObjective: compare two instances that both support a general claim
questions.stem: Essay A devotes two pages to a man who commutes an hour each way before arguing that buses are underfunded. Essay B devotes two pages to a woman who walks forty minutes to work before making the same argument. Which comparison is best supported?

options.text: Both are instances carrying a general claim, and they differ in what a reader can check, since one reader can inspect the bus route and the other only hear of the walk
Only A is using the instance properly, since an instance of a service that runs bears on its funding and an instance of a service that is missing does not
options.misconception: sets a rule about what counts as evidence, which the walker's case satisfies as much as the commuter's

options.text: Both argue by example and the difference is only in length, since two pages is enough in either case for a single person to carry a general claim
options.misconception: makes length the only variable, when the two cases support the same claim in different ways

options.text: A's instance is stronger because a funded service can be seen and B's is weaker because a walk cannot be, so the two are not equally good evidence
options.misconception: ranks instances by how visible they are, when a claim about funding is established by either case

questions.explanation: The two essays are doing the same thing and the interesting difference is in what a reader is asked to believe. A walk is a fact about one woman's forty minutes, and believing it requires taking her word for it, though the forty minutes is exactly what the claim predicts a person would do when there is no bus worth using. A commuter's hour is also one man's hour, but a reader can get on the bus, and the essay's two pages make a check possible that the walker cannot invite. That makes A the easier essay to argue with, not the stronger one, and the difference is one of accessibility rather than of fit. The second option invents a rule about evidence and applies it asymmetrically, and a walk is precisely the case a claim about inadequate provision predicts. The third reduces the comparison to a measurement of length. The fourth is the error the pair is built to catch, since a claim about how service is funded does not become true by being visible, and the case nobody can check is not thereby the weaker case.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can do with each case besides believing it.

questions.topic: The risk a digression runs
questions.learningObjective: state the risk a digression creates for a reader
questions.stem: An essay arguing for a restored library budget spends its third paragraph on how the town lost the last one, including the committee that closed it and the argument they had in 1974. What risk does that paragraph run?

options.text: That the reader is drawn into a second argument with its own villain and its own ending, and does not come back to the budget question the essay was written to settle
That the reader finds the history more persuasive than the present case and concludes that the essay's own position is the one that lost in 1974
options.misconception: supposes the reader is persuaded by the history, when the risk is losing the thread of the question

options.text: That the dates in the paragraph are checked and found wrong, which would make a reader distrust the figures in the rest of the essay as well
options.misconception: makes the danger a matter of dates, which is a correctness problem rather than a structural one

options.text: That the paragraph is too short to be worth the space, so the abruptness of the return is noticed more readily than the point of the return
options.misconception: treats the question as one of proportion, whereas a digression's danger is structural at any length

questions.explanation: The paragraph is not merely background; it has a subject, a cast and a resolution, and those are the ingredients of an argument in their own right. A committee with an argument to have, in a year with a date attached, gives a reader a shape to follow and a person to blame, and a reader who has spent a paragraph inside a shape wants the ending of it. The question is where that ending is, and if the paragraph supplies one, the essay has two conclusions and the reader has to guess which one the title promised. The second option assumes the reader is won over by the history, which is a failure the essay could correct by writing it better; the structural risk survives good writing. The third mistakes an accuracy problem for a structural one, and while a wrong date is worth correcting it does not restructure the paragraph. The fourth is the same error from the other side, treating the difficulty as one of length, when a short digression with its own ending is exactly as capable of taking the thread away.
questions.hint: Ask whether the paragraph supplies an ending of its own.

questions.topic: A digression that declares its purpose
questions.learningObjective: analyse how a declared digressation protects an essay's argument
questions.stem: An essay on a vanished theatre interrupts itself: "Before any of this, the theatre had a name, and the name was on the tickets, and I want to say something about the name, because the name is the argument." What has the interruption done for the essay?

options.text: It has told the reader what the interruption is for before giving it, so the reader has a reason to follow and the return is promised rather than merely performed
It has given the theatre a character, so the essay develops its subject in a register the main argument does not use and could not use
options.misconception: turns a subject into a person, when the interruption is offered as a piece of the argument

options.text: It has left the essay's structure in doubt, so a reader has to work out whether the name is evidence for the position or a substitute for it
options.misconception: reports confusion as the effect, though the sentence supplies the reason in its own final clause

options.text: It has held the argument back so the reader can enjoy the memory, so the pause is a gift before the case resumes as it was
options.misconception: reads the interruption as a pleasure rather than as part of the case

A writer who pauses in an argument takes on a debt, because the reader was somewhere else and now is not, and the only thing that keeps the debt from falling due is a reason given in advance. The third describes a text that withholds its reasons; this one states its reason in the same breath as the subject, which is why the doubt is unlikely and, in any case, is not what the sentence does. questions.topic: The work done by a parenthetical aside

questions.stem: An essay on libraries runs, "The county has eleven branches (three of them, as of last month, in buildings with no step-free entrance) and it has never published a count of visitors." What is the parenthesis doing?

It is supplying evidence for the claim that follows it, so a reader is handed a fact to set against the county's silence about the count
options.misconception: reads the qualification as support for a later claim, when it belongs to the figure before it

options.text: It is marking a concession, so the writer is admitting a weakness in the figure before making the larger accusation about the count
options.misconception: takes a qualification for a concession, which admits an argument's weakness rather than a fact's incompleteness

options.text: It is translating a term, so that a reader who does not know the word branches is given its sense in the words the county itself would use
options.misconception: supposes a term the sentence gives no sign of needing to be explained

Three of the eleven are inaccessible, which means the figure eleven is a fact about buildings rather than about service, and the essay cannot pause the sentence to say so without losing the momentum that carries it into the second clause. The third is the standing confusion between a qualification and a concession, and the difference is what each is directed at: a concession weakens the argument's case, a qualification narrows a fact. questions.topic: Two essays compared by the weight of their qualifications
questions.learningObjective: compare two essays by whether their qualifications are load-bearing
questions.stem: Essay A runs four paragraphs with no parentheses and two qualifying subordinate clauses. Essay B has eleven parentheses, and every one of them contains a figure or a date the surrounding sentence could not be read without. Which comparison is best supported?

B is the better written, since a writer willing to correct a figure in the middle of a sentence is more attentive than one who lets an imprecision stand
options.misconception: turns a practice into a verdict on quality, which is exactly what the pair is arranged to hold apart

options.text: A parenthesised note and a subordinate clause interrupt a sentence in different ways, so the two essays are not comparable and no comparison should be made

options.text: B is the more digressive of the two, since an essay that corrects itself eleven times cannot hold a line long enough to argue a position at all

The third declares the mechanisms incomparable, which is the refusal the pair forbids, since the question is what the qualifications do. questions.topic: Why an essay restates a claim
questions.learningObjective: explain what a restatement of a claim is doing for a reader
questions.stem: An essay's fourth paragraph says, "The library should be funded properly," and its seventh says, "Proper funding is what the library should have." Which is the better account of why the second sentence is there?

options.text: It re-establishes the claim after three paragraphs of evidence, so the restatement tells a reader that the argument has travelled back to its point
It says the same thing in fewer words, so a writer who has been wordy has improved the essay by supplying the shorter version of the first sentence
options.misconception: treats a repetition placed late in the argument as an act of editing, which is a different kind of correction

options.text: It makes a claim about the library rather than about funding, so the two sentences are not in fact the same claim expressed differently
options.misconception: claims a distinction between the two sentences that their wording does not make

options.text: It is a concession, since returning to an earlier claim after a page of evidence is the ordinary way a writer admits the claim was overstated
options.misconception: reads a return to the claim as an admission, which would need the wording to have weakened

questions.explanation: A restatement is placed where a reader has most likely forgotten, and its work depends on where that is. Three paragraphs of evidence sit between the two sentences, and evidence is exactly the material that carries a reader away from the claim it supports, so by the seventh paragraph a reader is holding figures and may no longer be holding the proposal. The second sentence puts the claim back in front of them at the moment the essay needs to use it again, and the phrasing is different in the useful way that marks it as a return rather than a repetition. The third invents a distinction; funding and the library are what the two sentences are about, in either order. The fourth is a category error, since a concession weakens a claim and this sentence strengthens the writer's hold on it.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is holding after the three paragraphs in between.

questions.topic: One sentence used twice, in two positions
questions.learningObjective: compare two uses of an identical sentence and account for the difference
questions.stem: Essay A's sixth paragraph reads, "The hall needs money," a sentence A has already used in its first and third paragraphs. Essay B's sixth paragraph reads the same words, and B has said nothing like it in five paragraphs. What distinguishes the two?

options.text: Nothing in the sentences themselves; what differs is how far each reader has travelled, so B's reader needs the claim returned and A's reader does not
A's sentence is redundant and B's is not, since repeating a claim spends space that a short essay cannot spare and a longer one can afford to waste
options.misconception: judges redundancy by the length of the essay rather than by how far the reader has come

options.text: B's sentence is an introduction, since a claim appearing for the first time in a sixth paragraph must be introducing a topic rather than returning to one
options.misconception: reads a first statement as an introduction, though the claim is the essay's from the start

options.text: A's sentence is a summary and B's is a new section, since a paragraph returning to an essay's claim is summarising while a first statement is beginning
options.misconception: assigns the two sentences different jobs when the only real difference is what preceded them

questions.explanation: A word-for-word repetition has no meaning of its own; it takes its meaning from the position, and the two positions are not equivalent. A reader of A has been given the claim three times and is now somewhere in the middle of its support, so a fourth use tells a reader nothing except that the writer has lost the thread. A reader of B has spent five paragraphs inside somebody's reasons and has not been told what they are reasons for, and the sentence converts all of that into an argument by naming what it is about. The second option is the ordinary view from outside, and it treats the space between two occurrences as if it were the same space in both cases, which it is not. The third treats a claim as a topic, and a topic is what a piece is about throughout rather than something introduced in paragraph six. The fourth gives the two different grammatical jobs, and nothing in the sentences supports a distinction between summarising and beginning; a sentence is a summary or an introduction in relation to what has come before, and that relation is exactly what differs.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader knows at the sixth paragraph in each essay.
