questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The price of a claim stated at the end
questions.learningObjective: evaluate what a closing position costs and buys in an essay
questions.stem: An essay argues both sides for eight paragraphs, states no position until its last two, and then claims that the town should keep its library open. What does that placement cost, and what does it buy?

options.text: It costs a reader who is being tested against something, and it buys a conclusion that arrives as the result of the weighing rather than as the premise of it
It costs the essay its argument, since a reader who does not know the position cannot follow the reasoning that is being used to reach one
options.misconception: assumes a reader must be told the position in order to follow reasoning, which is not true of a weighing of considerations

options.text: It buys suspense, since withholding the claim keeps a reader curious and a reader who is curious will read to the end to be told
options.misconception: turns a cost into a benefit the writer was aiming at, when suspense is what the placement produces rather than what it secures

options.text: It costs the writer any chance to be wrong early, since a claim stated at the end cannot be revised in the light of what the evidence turns out to show
options.misconception: supposes an early claim would have been revised, though a position can be defended or given up wherever it is stated

questions.explanation: A reader can follow two things at once: a sequence of considerations, which is what eight paragraphs of both sides are, and a claim that those considerations are about. Withholding the claim costs the second, because each paragraph must then be read as interesting in itself, and a reader who cannot tell what a paragraph is for is more likely to lose the thread than to be held by the suspense. What the placement buys is real and is the ordinary reason for it: a claim stated last is the conclusion of a weighing, and a reader receives it as the outcome of what they have just read, where a claim stated first is a premise the essay then tries to support and can fail to. The second option overstates the cost, since a reader can follow reasoning whose destination is undeclared, which is most of what people do when they read a case being argued. The third makes a by-product into a purpose. The fourth is confused about revision, which is what a writer does before publication, and a claim placed early can be withdrawn later just as easily as one placed late.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader is reading each paragraph for.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Paragraphs restored to the order of a late claim
questions.learningObjective: restore the order of paragraphs in an essay whose claim comes last
questions.stem: Four paragraphs from an invented essay whose claim is reached at the end have been printed out of order. Restore them so that each paragraph can only follow from the one before it.

options.text: and this is the reason the second petition was refused, which nobody at the time could say
and the committee's own minutes, which record two votes in favour of the closure
and the closure in 1991 was decided in eleven minutes, according to a document nobody has read
and none of this is an argument for the hall staying shut, which is the claim I want to reach

questions.explanation: The four paragraphs form a single chain of references, and each of them names something the one before it has supplied. The document comes first because nothing else can be mentioned until the reader knows that a document exists, and its obscurity is the fact the rest of the chain will do work with. The minutes come second because the document is the reason to look for them, and two votes in favour is the detail that makes the eleven minutes legible as a decision rather than an accident of procedure. The explanation of the refusal comes third, because a refusal needs a petition to have been refused, and the phrase nobody at the time could say depends on the reader already knowing the committee was tight-lipped. The last paragraph comes last because it is the only one that states where the chain has arrived, and it can say none of this is an argument precisely because the reader has just seen what this is. The order as printed puts the conclusion second, which is why the refusal appears to be explained before anything has been established to explain.
questions.hint: Find the paragraph that names the document, since nothing can refer to it before it exists.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a title sets up
questions.learningObjective: explain the expectation a title establishes for a reader
questions.stem: An essay is titled "The Committee Knew." Its first paragraph concerns a list of repairs a school needed and never received, and its last concerns how that list was compiled. What has the title set up for a reader?

options.text: An expectation of a story about people who could have acted, so every paragraph is read as evidence about a group's state of mind rather than as repair work
A promise of a single fact, since a title names its subject and a reader is entitled to find that subject examined rather than interpreted on the way
options.misconception: reads a title as a topic, when a title of this kind is an assertion and can be checked against what follows

options.text: An argument against the school, since the word knew makes a claim about knowledge and so implies a blame the essay is going to develop and defend
options.misconception: assumes the title's implication is the essay's argument, which the essay keeps in reserve

options.text: A rule about the essay's length, since a short title signals a short piece and a reader may reasonably stop before reaching the evidence
options.misconception: treats a title as a signal about length rather than about the kind of claim being made

questions.explanation: A title this short is an assertion, and the assertion is about a state of mind. The committee knew is a claim that somebody had the information and did not act on it, and every paragraph that follows is read against that claim whether or not the writer wants it to be: a paragraph about a repair list becomes evidence about what the list was for, and a paragraph about how the list was compiled becomes evidence about who was listening. That is a title doing work rather than labelling, because it tells a reader what kind of thing this is going to be and hands them a standard to hold it to. The second option is the topic reading, and it is defeated by the fact that a title can be checked: nothing in the word knew can be examined and found wanting the way a subject can. The third mistakes an implication for an argument, which is a difference of degree that matters, since an essay can keep its reader suspicious of a school without ever blaming one. The fourth is the length reading, and a short title says nothing about how long the piece is.
questions.hint: Ask whether the title could be proved false by the essay's contents.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Why a title cannot be a heading
questions.learningObjective: explain what a provisional title does that a subject heading cannot
questions.stem: An essay is titled "Notes Toward a History of the Allotment." Its first three paragraphs describe the writer's own repeated failures to grow anything, and its last paragraph argues that allotment waiting lists are the only surviving record of who wanted land. Explain what the title is doing for the essay, and why the essay needed a title rather than a subject heading.

answer.exemplar: The title is doing three separable things, and each of them instructs a reader about how to take what follows. Notes Toward is a declaration of incompleteness that changes the standard of success: an essay making notes can be unfinished without being faulty, so the writer may spend three paragraphs on personal failure without the reader demanding that it pay off, because the title has already said that it is material rather than argument. A History is a claim about what a history of this thing would be made of, and the last paragraph supplies the claim and tests it, so the title has staked something that the essay is free to answer or to fail. The Allotment names the object and holds the two at a distance that the three opening paragraphs then spend. A subject heading could do only the third of these. History of the Allotment would tell a reader the topic and would oblige the essay to survey it, and a survey is exactly what the essay is not offering, since its argument is that the usual sources are the wrong ones. The example above names the three functions, ties the incomplete note to the standard it sets, and says what a heading would have promised instead, because an explanation that stopped at the theme would describe the words without showing what a reader can do with them.

questions.explanation: An explanation of a title has to separate the things a title can do, because the temptation is to treat all of them as a single matter of subject matter and then to say the title is apt. The first thing to name is the claim of scope, since a history is a claim about what a history consists of and the essay's last paragraph makes that claim explicit, so the title and the conclusion are testing each other. The second is the declaration of provisionality, and this is the part with an effect on the reading rather than on the content: notes toward tells a reader how to treat the first three paragraphs, which otherwise look like an indulgence. The third is the ordinary naming of an object, which a heading also does. Having separated them, the explanation has to say why the essay could not be headed instead, and the answer lies in what a heading promises: a survey, complete and impersonal, where this essay is partial, personal and argumentative. The trap is the sentence that says the title is interesting.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader is told to expect by each of the three parts of the title.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a subtitle adds
questions.learningObjective: explain what a subtitle contributes beyond a title
questions.stem: A book is titled "The Long Field" and subtitled "A History of Allotments in One County, 1848 to 1937." What has the subtitle added to what the title promised?

options.text: A qualification, since the title names an experience and the subtitle bounds it to a single county and two dates, which is the limit of what the book can claim
A second argument, since a title makes a claim and a subtitle supplies the evidence that supports it, which is why the two have to be printed separately
options.misconception: divides a claim from its evidence, which is a job for a later chapter rather than for the line under the title

options.text: A description for a seller, since a subtitle is what a bookseller needs in order to place the book and it therefore belongs to the publisher rather than the writer
options.misconception: reduces a subtitle to sales copy, though a county and two dates are claims about scope and not descriptions for a shelf

options.text: An alternative title, so that a reader who dislikes the first has a second to hold instead and the pair can be read as interchangeable options
options.misconception: treats the two lines as rival titles, whereas a subtitle qualifies the first and is not read on its own

questions.explanation: The title is expansive and the subtitle is the instrument that keeps it honest. The long field is an experience, capable of standing for a history of allotments in general, and one county between two dates is a boundary small enough to be worth the reader's attention and narrow enough to be defended, since a book that stays inside it can be shown to have covered what it promised. That is the whole function of a subtitle in this arrangement: it converts a claim that could mean anything into a claim a reader can hold the book to, and the fact that the qualification is a limitation is what makes it useful, because a reader who knows the limit can read the book knowingly. The second option makes the subtitle an apparatus of proof, and there is no reason a claim and its evidence could not occupy the same page. The third treats it as merchandising, which mistakes a statement about scope for a statement about the subject's usefulness to a bookseller. The fourth presents the two as equals, and a reader who picks up the book by the subtitle has been given a scope with no argument in it.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can hold the book to after reading the second line.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A subtitle the essay does not earn
questions.learningObjective: identify the part of a subtitle an essay cannot support
questions.stem: An essay is titled "Two Years of One Mill" and subtitled "A Ledger from 1889, and How Industry Really Worked." The essay prints the mill's payroll for two years and argues that the wages in it track a trade that the county's other records ignore. Which part of the subtitle does the essay not earn?

options.text: The second clause, since how industry really worked is a claim about a whole trade and two years of one employer's payroll can support a claim about one firm
The first clause, since a single year's ledger cannot establish a practice the essay then sets against records covering the whole of the county's trade
options.misconception: moves the objection to the clause that concedes a limitation, which is the honest part of the subtitle

options.text: The word really, since a title that corrects a misconception ought first to state the misconception and the essay never describes the account it corrects
options.misconception: singles out one word when the overreach is the whole clause that word belongs to

options.text: Neither clause, since subtitles are permitted to promise more than a book delivers and this essay has been honest about the reach of its evidence
options.misconception: treats over-claiming as a publishing convention, whereas a subtitle is a claim the essay has to meet

questions.explanation: The subtitle is honest about its evidence and reckless about its conclusion, and the difference is what the item turns on. One ledger from one year is a small thing well described, and the first clause says so, which is why a reader knows at once what kind of book is on offer. The second clause then makes a claim no ledger can support: how industry really worked is a statement about a trade, and the essay's own argument is that the trade is visible only in a particular narrow kind of record, so a reader who wanted the trade would need the very sources the essay says do not exist. The second option puts the objection on the clause that states the limit, which is a clause written in the essay's favour, since naming the evidence is what earns the reader's trust. The third isolates a word, but the overreach is the clause and the word is only the intensifier inside it. The fourth is the defence of a convention, and conventions are permissions, not claims; nothing about being a subtitle excuses a claim the evidence cannot reach.
questions.hint: Ask which clause claims more than the evidence described can support.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: What a closing image does
questions.learningObjective: explain the argumentative work performed by a closing image
questions.stem: An essay about municipal water ends by describing a standpipe at the end of a street, one tap, and a queue that forms at six in the morning. What is the closing image doing?

options.text: It is putting the claim into one place a reader can picture, so what the essay has argued about who bears a cost arrives as something seen rather than as a figure
It is repeating the essay's central term a last time, so a reader closes the piece still holding the vocabulary that the argument has built up and needed
options.misconception: reads a closing image as a repetition of a term, when nothing in the image is a term

options.text: It is supplying the piece of evidence the earlier paragraphs lacked, so the image completes the case and settles the question the essay opened by raising it
options.misconception: supposes new evidence, which a closing image cannot be, since everything in it has been described before

options.text: It is leaving the reader with a mood, so the essay ends on feeling because a feeling is what should be carried away rather than a settled conclusion
options.misconception: makes the ending a matter of mood, whereas the image is the claim in its most concrete available form

questions.explanation: An argument is made of figures, and figures are forgotten in a way that pictures are not. A reader who has been given a percentage will be able to say the number afterwards, and a reader who has been shown one tap with a queue at six in the morning will be able to see the distribution of inconvenience in a single place, at an hour that a council has to answer for. That is what a closing image does: it converts the essay's most general claim into the most particular thing the essay contains, and it is able to do that precisely because everything in it has been established already, so the image spends no reader's effort on new material and asks the reader only to see what has been argued. The second option is a reading of a different device; no term is being repeated, and vocabulary is not what an image carries. The third is the natural confusion, since an image does carry evidential weight, but nothing in it is new and a reader who had to learn a fact would be distracted at exactly the wrong moment. The fourth makes the ending a matter of atmosphere, which is the description of how the image feels and not of what it does.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader can now see that they could not see before the last paragraph.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Why a closing image takes three clauses
questions.learningObjective: explain how the structure of a closing image carries an argument
questions.stem: An essay about a village's lost orchard ends: "There are four trees left on the field, and the gate is open, and nobody in the village knows which four." Explain what that last sentence does to the argument the essay has made, and why it is built from three clauses rather than one.

answer.exemplar: The sentence gathers the essay's claim into a single concrete instance, and the three clauses are the stages by which a reader arrives at it. The first clause supplies the fact the whole essay has been accumulating towards, four trees where there were a hundred and forty, and stated plainly it is the only arithmetic left in the sentence. The second clause does something the fact alone cannot: the gate is open, so the remaining trees are not protected, and the reader is made to see that the loss is finished rather than continuing, which is the difference between a disaster that has happened and a situation that continues. The third clause is the argument's real conclusion, and it is not about trees at all. Nobody in the village knows which four means that no one is left who could restore what is left, because the list of who cared has gone with the people on it, so a reader who arrives at an open gate expecting an inheritance finds an absence of heirs. Three clauses are necessary because the argument has three stages: what remains, what has stopped being done about it, and who is left to do it. A single clause would have to choose one, and the one the sentence withholds is the one the essay exists to make. The example above names each clause's work and says why the order is fixed, because an explanation that reported the image without unpacking the stages would leave a reader admiring a sentence they could not use.

questions.explanation: An explanation of a closing sentence has to do two things: say what the sentence concludes, and say why it is built the way it is. The conclusion is the argumentative half and the structure is the analytical half, and an explanation that only gives the first is describing an ending rather than explaining one. The structure has to be accounted for clause by clause, because each clause does a distinct job and the order is not interchangeable: a fact about what remains, a fact about what has stopped, and a fact about who is left. The temptation is to explain a closing image as a matter of tone, which is a description of pleasure rather than of reasoning, and it is also to treat the three clauses as one long sentence whose length is expressive, when the clauses could not be rearranged and the last one is doing the work the essay has been preparing. A second temptation is to say the image restates the essay's claim, which is true and useless, because the question is what the claim looks like when it has been said this way.
questions.hint: Ask what each clause adds that the one before it did not.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A claim refuted by the essay's own paragraph
questions.learningObjective: identify self-contradiction between a claim and the evidence offered for it
questions.stem: An essay claims, "Nobody in this town books a holiday in August." Its second paragraph notes that in the holiday week of 1998 both of the town's guesthouses stood empty, and its third paragraph observes that a third of the town's households are away in the second week of August. What has the essay done?

options.text: It has gathered evidence that refutes its own claim, since a third of the households being away in August is the strongest possible support for a full August and it is being offered against itself
It has offered evidence too thin to settle a universal claim, so the argument fails for want of examples rather than because anything opposes it
options.misconception: makes the fault a shortage of cases when the essay contains a statement that defeats the claim outright

options.text: It has confused a national figure with a local one, so the third paragraph should be read as a claim about the country rather than about the town and the essay is sound
options.misconception: invents a confusion between two scales, which the paragraph about the town's own households does not introduce

options.text: It has worded the claim too strongly, so a reader who objects to the word nobody will stop reading and the essay's remaining evidence will go unread
options.misconception: blames the wording, which is a separate fault from a later paragraph refuting the claim

questions.explanation: The third paragraph does not weaken the case; it destroys it, and the reason is a matter of what the claim quantifies over. Nobody in this town books a holiday in August is a claim about every household in a place, and a statement that a third of those households are away in the second week of August is not a gap in the evidence but a positive instance of the thing the claim says does not happen. The guesthouse paragraph points the same way, since two empty guesthouses in the busiest week is not what a deserted August looks like, and a writer assembling evidence against a claim of universal absence has assembled it. The second option describes the commonest way a universal claim fails, which is by being supported only by a thin sample, and it is not what has happened here. The third option supplies a confusion between a country and a town that the paragraph does not contain, since the households are the town's own. The fourth is a real fault and it is beside the point: a reader who objects to nobody is doing exactly what the third paragraph licenses, and a more careful word would have been worse.
questions.hint: Ask whether the third paragraph is evidence for or against the first sentence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An argument defeated by its own material
questions.learningObjective: explain how a claim is defeated by evidence that appears to support it
questions.stem: A travel essay claims, "The town is best avoided in July," and supports the claim with three paragraphs about crowds in the first week of July. Its fourth paragraph then reports, in a tone of relief, that the town is empty in the second week. Explain how the essay's own material defeats the claim, and what a writer would have to do to make the claim good.

answer.exemplar: The claim is about a month and the evidence is about a week, and the fourth paragraph is what makes the difference impossible to ignore. Crowds in the first week of July are exactly what a claim about July would be expected to produce, so for three paragraphs the evidence and the claim look like partners. Then the second week is reported as empty, and a report of emptiness is not a neutral addition: it is a fact that the claim has to accommodate, and the claim cannot. Either the town is crowded in July, which the fourth paragraph denies, or it is not crowded in July, in which case the crowds of the first week were a local accident and the generalisation was never entitled to them. The tone of relief matters as much as the content, because a writer pleased to find the town empty is telling a reader how to weigh the finding, and the pleasure is inconsistent with the recommendation the essay is making. To make the claim good the writer has two honest routes and no third. The claim can be narrowed to the first week, and then the fourth paragraph becomes supporting detail about how short the season is. Or the emptiness can be explained, and the essay would have to say why an empty second week does not count as evidence against a claim about the town in high season, which is an argument about holiday weeks rather than about crowds. The example above names the mismatch of scope, the role of the tone, and the two repairs, because an explanation that stopped at the contradiction would leave the writer with no way forward.

questions.explanation: An explanation of an argument that defeats itself has to identify the mismatch precisely, name what the apparently supporting paragraphs are really doing, and give the repairs that would make the claim hold. The mismatch is one of scope, and it has to be stated as a mismatch between a month and a week rather than as a general vagueness, because a vague claim is repairable by sharpening and this one is not. The second requirement is the hardest, since the first three paragraphs read as support and the reader of the explanation has to be shown why they are not: a claim about July is licensed to draw on July, and drawing on the first week is a sample of the month, which is only evidence if the sample is representative, and the fourth paragraph is what shows it is not. The third requirement is the difference between an explanation and a complaint. Saying the claim is wrong leaves the writer with nothing, while naming the two repairs shows why the failure came from the claim's width rather than from its evidence. The trap is to call the fourth paragraph a contradiction, which is a word for a conflict between two assertions and misses that only one of them was ever made.
questions.hint: Ask how much of July the first three paragraphs actually cover.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Three books, one memoir
questions.learningObjective: decide which of three described books is a memoir
questions.stem: Three books are described. A covers a man's whole working life, ordered by the years he held each job. B covers the eleven months his wife was ill, and its last chapter is about a quarrel they had after her diagnosis. C covers the same whole working life but is arranged by the things he repaired in each house he lived in. Which is the memoir?

options.text: B, since a memoir is bounded by a stretch of experience and B's last chapter lies inside that stretch, where A and C both take in a life from end to end
C, since an autobiography is free to arrange itself and a memoir is not, and C's arrangement proves that it is the fuller of the two records
options.misconception: reverses the freedom of arrangement, which belongs to the autobiography and not to the memoir

options.text: A, since a memoir is written by someone looking back, and A is the only one of the three told in the order a life is lived
options.misconception: uses the order of narration as the test, which any of the three forms may adopt for any part of itself

options.text: All three are memoirs, since what separates memoir from autobiography is how honest the writer is rather than what the book is obliged to cover
options.misconception: grounds the distinction in the writer's sincerity, which is a claim about a person and not about a form

questions.explanation: The deciding question is what each book is obliged to cover, and only one of the three has taken on a stretch rather than a life. A's span is a working life and C's is the same span, and the difference between them, an arrangement by jobs in one and by repairs in the other, shows that a book covering a whole life is free to organise that life any way it likes. That freedom is available because the book is answering to the whole, and a book that has taken on a life cannot be rescued from its own gaps. B is bounded at both ends by an illness, and its last chapter is inside those bounds, so the quarrel is part of the stretch rather than a piece of a life survey. The second option reverses the arrangement, and it is worth noticing that C's arrangement is precisely the sort of thing a memoir does with the same material, where the repairs would stand in for the wife. The third mistakes the order of a life for the scope of a book. The fourth substitutes the writer's character for the book's obligation, which is a different kind of comment altogether.
questions.hint: Ask which book answers to a life and which to a stretch of it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A declared basis quietly replaced
questions.learningObjective: identify a comparison that has drifted off its declared basis
questions.stem: An essay announces that it will compare two novels by their treatment of inheritance, and by its fourth paragraph it is comparing the size of the two estates and the age of the two lawyers. What has happened to the basis?

options.text: It has been replaced, since the essay is now working by a different variable, and a reader who accepted the declared basis cannot check anything in the new material at all
It has been narrowed, since the size of an estate is a consequence of an inheritance and a comparison by consequence is still a comparison by inheritance
options.misconception: accepts a chain of cause as a basis, though a basis is what a comparison is organised by and not what produced its materials

options.text: It has been kept, since inheritance is what produced both the estate and the lawyer, so every fact downstream of it can serve the basis without displacing it
options.misconception: lets any related fact serve a declared basis, which would leave a basis with no power to constrain anything

options.text: It has been made sharper, since naming a concrete feature of an inheritance is the ordinary way a reader is given a handle on an abstract subject
options.misconception: reads specificity as clarity, when the facts named here belong to a different comparison from the one announced

questions.explanation: A declared basis is an agreement with the reader, and its whole value lies in being checkable. Having announced inheritance, the essay has undertaken that a reader will be able to take each finding and ask whether inheritance explains it, and the reader who has agreed has done a piece of work in exchange for the promise of an argument. The estate's size and the lawyer's age cannot be reached in that way, because a reader holding the basis of inheritance has nothing to compare them against, and the reader must now go back and find out what the essay is now comparing. That is the cost, and it is why a replaced basis is worse than a badly chosen one. The second option is a seductive defence, since the size of an estate genuinely does follow from an inheritance, but a comparison organised by cause is a different comparison from one organised by the way a text treats that cause. The third grants any related fact the standing of evidence for the declared basis, which would make a basis no constraint at all. The fourth mistakes making a thing concrete for keeping to a question.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader who accepted the announced basis can check the new material.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A counterargument answered by dating it
questions.learningObjective: evaluate an answer that disposes of a counterargument by its date
questions.stem: An essay argues for a longer school day. It sets out the strongest case against at length, and then answers it in a single sentence: the case against was made in 1990 and the conditions have changed. What does that answer fail to do?

options.text: It leaves the objection as it stands now unanswered, since a counterargument does not expire with the decade in which it was formulated, and it has to be met in its present form
It meets it, since dating an objection is a legitimate answer to one, and a reader who accepts the date has no further ground left to stand on
options.misconception: mistakes a temporal objection for a refutation, which is what dating the argument in effect does

options.text: It fails only on space, since a counterargument given three paragraphs has been answered in one sentence and the essay has weighted its own position more heavily
options.misconception: makes the deficit one of space, whereas a counterargument can be answered at any length if the answer meets it

options.text: It misidentifies what is in dispute, because the case against concerns the length of the day while the essay has answered a claim about the 1990s instead
options.misconception: supposes a mismatch of subjects, which nothing in the exchange exhibits

questions.explanation: The answer works on a reader who accepts one particular premise, and the premise is that a claim belongs to the moment it was made. Where that premise holds, dating the objection is a complete answer, because it says the world has moved and the reasoning has not. But that premise is exactly what is in question when a case against a longer school day is being made now, since the reasons usually given for the objection, that children are tired, that teachers cannot plan, that the last hour is a waste, are reasons that have not gone out of date and that the essay has not touched. An answer which leaves the strongest form of the objection standing has not disposed of it, and a reader who wants to know what follows for the present is no better served than a reader who was never shown the objection. The second option takes the answer at its strongest and calls it sufficient, which requires the reader to grant the premise. The third makes it a matter of proportion, and the length of an answer is not what makes it an answer. The fourth supplies a mismatch of subjects that the exchange does not contain.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader who still thinks the 1990 argument is right should conclude.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Six paragraphs of family history inside an argument
questions.learningObjective: analyse the cost of a digression that does not announce its return
questions.stem: An essay about a town's buses opens its third paragraph, "My grandfather drove one of these for twenty-two years," and does not come back to the service until the ninth. What has the passage cost the essay?

options.text: Six paragraphs with the reader inside a family history, and on the return the essay has to remind a reader who has been elsewhere what the original question was about buses at all
Only space, since the story is worth hearing and an essay may spend a paragraph on anything provided the argument eventually resumes as before
options.misconception: measures the cost in space alone, when a reader can be six paragraphs away from the question

options.text: The reader's sympathy, since a grandfather who drove a bus is a likelier figure than an argument about a service and the essay's case is outcompeted by him
options.misconception: supposes the reader has taken a side, whereas the difficulty is that the reader no longer knows what is being asked

options.text: Nothing, since a personal paragraph at the start of a non-fiction essay is an established manner and a reader will not be lost by one paragraph
options.misconception: treats a convention as a guarantee, and the passage here runs to six paragraphs rather than one

questions.explanation: The paragraph is not merely personal, it is a subject with its own duration, and twenty-two years is a fact that opens questions the essay is not going to answer. Once a reader has been given a man, a machine and a span of years, the six paragraphs that follow are read as biography, and a reader who has spent that long inside somebody's working life is not tracking an argument about the service they were promised in the first two paragraphs. The return therefore has a cost of its own, which is the ninth paragraph's opening moves: the essay has to reconstruct the question before it can use the material it gathered, and whatever that reconstruction takes is not available for the argument. The second option measures the cost in space and lets everything else go, which is the standard defence and the reason digressions are defended at all. The third substitutes a different trouble, a reader persuaded of something, when the problem is that the reader is lost rather than converted. The fourth treats a manner as a guarantee of effect, and the guarantee of a convention is that a reader expects a return, which is precisely what has not been given.
questions.hint: Ask what the ninth paragraph has to do before the argument can continue.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two ways of reaching a position
questions.learningObjective: compare an accumulated position with a posited one
questions.stem: Essay A reaches its position in the ninth paragraph after three images, and calls those images what it has instead of a reason. Essay B states its position in the third paragraph and then defends it for six more. Which comparison of the two arrivals is best supported?

options.text: A's is reached by accumulation and is a claim about the absence of grounds, where B's is a premise the remaining six paragraphs are working from
A's is weaker because it comes later, and a reader who has waited nine paragraphs has learned nothing that the third paragraph of B would not have given sooner
options.misconception: measures support by the speed of arrival, which is a claim about a reader's patience and not about evidence

options.text: A's is better supported, since three images are harder to dismiss than six paragraphs of reasoning and a reader is more easily moved by what is shown than by what is argued
options.misconception: prefers the concrete without asking what the images are evidence of

options.text: The two are the same kind of thing, since a position stated after evidence and a position stated before it are one claim in a different order of sentences
options.misconception: assumes the two positions are one claim, which the ninth paragraph's own account of itself denies

questions.explanation: The two essays differ in what their positions are for, and the difference is visible in how each uses the paragraphs that follow. B's position is a premise: it is stated early precisely so that six paragraphs can be spent on it, and a reader who disagrees has a specific place to enter the essay. A's position is a conclusion and a diagnosis at once, since the ninth paragraph does not merely state where the images have led but claims that they have led there without grounds, which is a claim about the essay's own method and can only be made at the end. The second option measures support by when it arrives, and a reader's patience is not evidence; an argument delivered in the third paragraph can be as unfounded as one in the ninth. The third asserts that the concrete is always the stronger case, which the ninth paragraph is busy denying. The fourth reduces the two to an order of sentences, and an order of sentences is exactly what separates a premise from a conclusion.
questions.hint: Ask what each essay does with the paragraphs after the position is stated.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: One claim three times against one claim once
questions.learningObjective: compare two essays by how they place a claim in the reading
questions.stem: Essay A states its claim in the second paragraph, returns to it in the sixth, and restates it in the last. Essay B states its claim once, in the eighth paragraph, and never repeats it. Which comparison is best supported?

options.text: A's repetitions report where the argument has reached, where B's single statement has to be read back against six paragraphs of reasoning before a reader can say what they are for
A's repetitions are padding, since a claim stated three times occupies three times the space and gives a reader nothing they did not have at the second statement
options.misconception: counts repetitions as waste, when a repetition can report the argument's position at a stage

options.text: B's single statement is stronger, because a claim made once cannot be weakened by a later restatement and so the position is guaranteed to hold throughout
options.misconception: treats a single statement as a guarantee, whereas a position stated once can be abandoned later without comment

options.text: The two essays are equivalent, since what matters is a reader's memory of the claim and restatement is only a way of helping a reader who forgets easily
options.misconception: reduces both to an aid to memory, and a claim's place in an argument is not a memory problem

questions.explanation: A claim is a promise about the rest of the essay, and the two essays make it at different moments and honour it in different ways. A tells a reader what the essay is for within a paragraph or two and then renews the promise twice, which converts each renewal into a report: by the sixth the reader knows what has been established and what remains, and by the last the reader knows the argument has closed. B withholds the promise until the eighth, and everything before it is reasoning whose purpose a reader has to infer and then hold. Neither is defective, but they impose different reading, and A's reader is told what to expect while B's reader is asked to supply it. The second option counts the repetitions as space, which is the cost and not the function. The third mistakes repetition for vulnerability; a single statement is easily abandoned later without anyone noticing, which is a weakness rather than a strength. The fourth reduces the arrangements to memory aids, and what is at stake in both essays is the reader's orientation rather than their recall.
questions.hint: Ask what each essay tells a reader to expect, and when.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An image against a repeated phrase
questions.learningObjective: compare two closings by the argumentative work each performs
questions.stem: Essay A ends with an image of a single unlit street. Essay B ends by returning to the phrase it began with and repeating it exactly. Which of the two closings is doing more argumentative work?

options.text: A's, since an image states a claim in a form a reader cannot argue with, where a repeated phrase marks a shape finished and adds nothing to the case being made
B's, since a return to the opening phrase closes the argument formally, and formal closure is what a reader needs in order to accept a conclusion
options.misconception: prefers formal closure, which is a property of an essay's shape rather than of the case that shape carries

options.text: A's, since images are stronger than restatements in every case, and an essay should trust its reader to complete a claim from a picture alone
options.misconception: asserts a hierarchy of endings without asking what each one has to do with the claim

options.text: Neither, since both closings are conventional and a conventional closing is a neutral one that puts no additional weight on either argument
options.misconception: takes convention to cancel effect, where a convention may be used to mean a particular thing in a particular essay

questions.explanation: A closing has to leave the reader holding the argument rather than merely aware that it has stopped, and the two devices work on different things. An image puts the claim into the one form a reader cannot negotiate with, because a street with no light in it is not a proposition and cannot be answered; a reader who disputes it has to say what should be there, and by then the essay has won the point it was making. A repeated phrase is a statement about shape, and its value is real but narrower: it tells a reader the piece is over and returns them to where they began, which is a satisfaction rather than an argument. The second option is the standard defence of the formal ending and it confuses the frame with the content, since a reader does not accept a conclusion because the architecture closed neatly. The third is a generalisation about devices that the pair exists to complicate, since an image that misstates the case argues for nothing. The fourth assumes convention is inert, and conventions are available precisely because a reader recognises them and expects a particular use.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader can argue with what each ending has placed in front of them.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Repair steps restored to their order
questions.learningObjective: restore the order of steps in a process essay about repairing a cover
questions.stem: Four steps from an invented essay on repairing a torn book cover have been printed out of order. Restore them so that each step is possible only after the one before it.

options.text: and I pressed the whole thing flat under a heavy box for a month
and I cleaned the board with a cloth and left it to dry overnight
and I cut away the loose spine with a small knife, working from the middle outward
and I laid the paper back down and left the corners to be fixed another day

questions.explanation: The four steps are a repair, and a repair has an order fixed by what each stage makes possible. The cutting comes first because nothing else can be done while the spine is still attached, and working from the middle outward is what keeps the tear from running while the knife is in it. Cleaning and drying come second, and drying is the condition the next step needs: a board that has been wiped and left overnight will take weight, and one that has been wiped and used at once will not. Pressing comes third, and a month under a box is what removes the moisture the drying began on, so the sequence has a duration rather than a mere order. Laying the paper back down comes last, and it is last because it is the step the others prepared the surface for; the corners are left for another day because a corner needs a dry board and a board needs pressing, and the essay is honest about leaving work undone rather than pretending to a completeness it did not reach. The order as printed begins at the press, which is why the first step looked possible on its own.
questions.hint: Find the step without which the surface cannot be worked on at all.
